h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: Because the L2 gradient is divided by batch size and applied every step, effective per-epoch decay scales like alpha*N/B^2, so at batch sizes 4-10 raising alpha over-shrinks weights and causes underfitting.
Under standard parametrization Adam moves each weight by about lr, so layer-output changes grow with fan-in and wide nets destabilize sooner as the learning rate rises.
Per-weight data gradients shrink with width while the L2 pull does not, so at alpha 0.129-1 extra width increases the relative regularization and pushes toward underfitting.
At learning rates 0.0774-1, larger batches reduce gradient noise and the number of risky steps, partially rescuing near-divergent training, whereas elsewhere they mainly cost update steps.
At high learning rates per-layer perturbations multiply through depth, so adding layers turns marginal stability into divergence.
The strong effective L2 at batch sizes 4-10 shrinks every layer, and the shrinkage compounds multiplicatively as layers are added.
Large batches give few steps per epoch and low-noise gradients, so they both need and tolerate a larger learning rate to converge within the budget.
With strong L2 every added layer's weights shrink and the product of shrunken layers collapses the signal, so depth hurts under high alpha.
With one hidden layer width is the only capacity route, so narrowing hurts more than in deeper nets where depth compensates.
When layers are narrow (16-40 units), added depth supplies compositional capacity that relieves the width bottleneck.
